episode_summary: August 2020 Hashing It Out episode with Lucas Geiger and Zaki Manian about Open Libra, a cypherpunk response to Facebook's Libra. They discuss Libra's Tendermint-like design, consensus scaling limits, full reserve bank and too-big-to-fail risks, stablecoin models, and whether blockchain can deliver value to ordinary users.

cards.claim: In August 2020 Lucas Geiger said Libra was going to be a walled garden where any collateral in the network could be seized at any time.
cards.speaker: Lucas Geiger
cards.quote: it was going to be a wallet garden. and that any amount of collateral that you had in the Libra network could be sort of seized at any time

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Facebook's Libra team had re-implemented an extremely similar design to Tendermint, which the Cosmos team had been getting production ready in 2018.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: of engineers re-implementing exactly, basically, an extremely similar design, a design that was inspired by Jay's earlier work.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest described Tendermint's BFT consensus as a near-optimal implementation of classical BFT that scales to hundreds or thousands of nodes.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: which is sort of just a nearly optimal implementation of and like robust implementation of classical BFT consensus that easily scales to hundreds and thousands of nodes

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest argued consensus protocols were essentially over as the interesting problem, with economics and coordination now the frontier.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: consensus protocols are, I think, essentially over in terms of what I think of as, like, important, interesting pieces.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the biggest blocker was use cases willing to pay for on-chain transactions, not consensus technology.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: But right now, we're struggling right now to have use cases that are willing to spend the money needed to put transactions on chain.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Libra's economic distribution was a handful of hyperscale corporations and venture capitalists holding equity, which was the only path to governance.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: the economic distribution of Facebook is a handful of hyperscale corporations and venture capitalists that have an equity interest in this equivalent of a Swiss LLC.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest warned that Libra governance could evict a developer from the Libra blockchain, wiping out their investment in that stack.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: The open the Libra governance can evict you from the Libra blockchain and all of your investment in that technical stack, in that knowledge, expertise, et cetera, goes away.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Libra's overall design was a full reserve bank, which lends out none of its deposits.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: But I think the overall design of the Libra ecosystem is designed as a full reserve bank.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest explained that a full reserve bank does not lend out deposits, so it earns no interest and must charge fees to users.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: But the appeal of the full reserve bank is that they don't lend out any capital.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Libra users would have to buy coins through an authorized reseller such as Coinbase, which would hold the dollars in the Facebook trust.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: they have to buy it through an authorized reseller, probably something like Coinbase.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Facebook could very easily hold a trillion dollars in Libra reserves, possibly ten trillion.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: Facebook could very easily get a trillion dollars in there

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest argued Libra would be a too-big-to-fail bank with no government able to bail it out, governed only by an investor LLC.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: That's that this one would really be the one type of bank that's too big to fail because there's nobody that could bail it out.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the US would have to rewrite a lot of its banking regulations to stop Libra.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: The US would probably have to rewrite a lot of its banking regulations to be able to stop Libra.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest argued that banks and technology companies were both trying to become each other, which was the bigger story.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: companies and technology companies are trying to become banks. I think that's the bigger story that's going on.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the Federal Reserve's origin was a group of upstart technology-savvy financial firms seizing power from state governments and legacy banks.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: The origin of the Federal Reserve system is a group of upstart technologically significant financial firms seizing power from both the state governments

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the Federal Reserve was privately created and is still a private entity.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: still is a private entity. So A, okay, this has all happened before.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest predicted Open Libra would be an easier sell than Facebook's Libra.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I actually see a project like Open Libra being an easier sell than Facebook's Libra.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest predicted Libra would either shift the narrative in Facebook's favor and reach production, or Facebook would partner with a successful copycat.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: will shift um in facebook's favor and you'll see something that uh that you know more closely resembles what they proposed this year in terms of libra actually getting into production

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest predicted that hundreds of corporate copies of Libra would appear and that one would succeed, with Facebook possibly partnering with it.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: you know eventually one will succeed and facebook may just partner with the whoever succeeds or the top three that succeed

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said something like Libra seemed inevitable even if it did not come directly from Facebook.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: they've already created enough space that something like Libra seems to me to be inevitable even if it doesn't directly come from Libra.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest estimated that a community of about 100,000 people could easily pay the administration costs of an affinity-group stablecoin network.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I think that's sort of the population of 100,000 people could easily pay for the administration costs of an organization like this.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said stablecoins differ by who pays for stability: the network in the Libra and Circle models, or the borrower in the MakerDAO-style model.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: there are two ways to think about stable coins, generally speaking, and it's about who pays for the stability.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest explained that in the Maker model the person taking the loan pays for stability and provides the capital, which scales and decentralizes differently.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And in that case, the person paying for the stability is actually the person taking the loan.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Facebook's stablecoin model was easy to implement, with administration costs lower than they seemed and strong legal precedent.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: The Facebook one is easy to implement and the administration costs are not actually that high as it might seem.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a host argued Libra only scaled to about 100 nodes because it uses classical consensus, and the guest called that nonsense.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: libra only scales but so much it scales to 100 nodes and that's because it is a classical protocol

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the Tendermint team ran 206 nodes during Game of Stakes at about the same block time as the Cosmos Hub.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: Tendermint at 206 nodes during Game of Stakes. And it was running at basically the same block time the Cosmos hub is running right now.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the real limit on proof-of-stake-style networks was paying node operators, not writing a consensus protocol for a million nodes.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: we don't really have a mechanism of economically rewarding paying for the operating costs incentivizing the sovereignty of even a few hundred nodes today.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest estimated that paying thousands of nodes would require networks worth on the order of a hundred billion dollars.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: You probably need something on the order of, you know, hundred billion dollar networks before you can even start getting into the realm

cards.claim: In August 2020 a host said IoT devices do not need to be consensus nodes, since they only need to send transactions through endpoints.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Your IoT device does not need to be a consensus node. It needs to be able to manually send transactions.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest praised Libra's mempool design as one of his favorite parts of the code, and said Tendermint would adopt it.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And Libra actually has a great mempool design. It's one of my favorite pieces of the code.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said the biggest problem in the industry was that developers build products for rich countries rather than for places that need blockchain.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: we have generally as an industry is that we're all trying to build products for ourselves in mostly rich countries

cards.claim: In August 2020 a host was skeptical that blockchain could offer much value to people in the United States or Europe.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: I'm actually quite skeptical that blockchain can offer much value for folks in the United States or in Europe.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said blockchain as it stood was a step down from current systems on user experience.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: is actually a step down from our current system from a user experience perspective.

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said Libra had a chance because it used classical consensus, which could help it get off the ground.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I think Libra has a chance because it is, A, using classical consensus protocols

cards.claim: In August 2020 a guest said day-to-day Bitcoin users still could not buy a coffee over the Lightning Network, despite promises.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: you can't buy a coffee through the lightning network like they promised

title: OpenLIbra - Lucas Geiger and Zaki Manian
